passage:
Senior manager's note. Shalini Menon, analytics division, Chennai. Annual review of Saurabh, team lead.
Saurabh, twenty-six, took over a team known for weekend work and high turnover. He changed three things. First, he stopped weekend emails, planning deadlines honestly instead. Second, he paired each new analyst with an experienced one for their first three months. Third, when a senior colleague publicly mocked a junior's mistake in a meeting, Saurabh spoke to him privately the same day and reported the pattern to HR. Output did not drop; it rose. Two people who had planned to resign stayed. He told me, "I'm not trying to be nice. I just don't want to build a team that breaks people." I've recommended him for the leadership programme and asked him to share his approach with other leads.

qa.q: For how long does each new analyst get paired with an experienced one?
qa.a: For their first three months.

qa.q: What might Saurabh have felt when the senior colleague mocked a junior?
qa.a: He likely felt angry and protective of the junior, which is why he acted the same day.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that showed sustainable, ethical leadership?
qa.a: He stopped weekend emails, set honest deadlines, paired new analysts with mentors and addressed a colleague's bullying.

qa.q: How might the two people who planned to resign see the team now?
qa.a: They likely feel respected and safer, which is why they chose to stay.

grounding: A manager's note records a young team lead building a healthy, ethical team culture.

passage:
Friday. Leela's journal.
Three months as manager. Today I did the thing I've been scared to do. In the team meeting, I said, "No more midnight replies. If it's urgent, call. Otherwise, it waits till morning." Everyone stared. My old boss used to email at 1 a.m. and expect answers by 7. I did that for two years. I nearly burned out. Avni, the newest analyst, came to my desk afterwards and whispered, "Thank you. I've been sleeping with my phone on my chest." That broke my heart a bit. I've started meeting her every Thursday to go through her work, the way I wish someone had done for me. I want to be good at this job without becoming someone who grinds people down.

qa.q: On which day does Leela meet Avni each week?
qa.a: Every Thursday.

qa.q: How did Leela feel before making the announcement?
qa.a: Leela felt scared to break the old midnight-reply habit.

qa.q: How is Leela building a healthier work culture?
qa.a: By ending midnight replies and mentoring Avni weekly, instead of repeating the old boss's habits.

qa.q: How might Avni feel after the meeting?
qa.a: Avni likely feels relieved and grateful, able to sleep without the phone on her chest.

grounding: A young manager's journal records ending an unhealthy late-night work culture and mentoring a junior.

passage:
To: Mr Wasim Qureshi, Heritage Cell, Municipal Corporation, Ahmedabad
Dear Sir,
I am writing about the old stepwell behind the Kalupur market. It is over three hundred years old and is now full of plastic and rubble. Last month, I organised a walk there with twenty college students. Many of them had never heard of it. We would like to propose a restoration drive: our volunteers can clear rubbish on weekends if the Corporation provides safety equipment and an engineer's guidance. We would also like to create a small signboard telling its history, in Gujarati and English, and guide school groups monthly. I have attached photographs and a plan. I would be grateful for a meeting.
Yours sincerely,
Pradeep Shah

qa.q: How old is the stepwell?
qa.a: Over three hundred years old.

qa.q: What might Pradeep be feeling while writing the letter?
qa.a: Pradeep likely feels concerned about the neglect and hopeful the Corporation will help.

qa.q: What makes Pradeep's proposal a responsible way to preserve heritage?
qa.a: It offers volunteers but asks for safety equipment and an engineer, and plans signboards and school visits for the next generation.

qa.q: How might the college students feel about the restoration drive?
qa.a: They may feel excited and proud to help save a piece of their city's history.

grounding: A young adult writes to a heritage officer proposing a volunteer restoration of an old stepwell.

passage: "Gurleen, you asked on your show why I started the song circle. I'm Nilesh, twenty-five. My Dadi knew over two hundred folk songs from our village near Bhilwara. Wedding songs, harvest songs, lullabies. When she died, I realised nobody had written them down. Most were gone. That hit me hard. So I went back and recorded every elder who still remembered anything. Sixty songs so far. Then I thought: recordings aren't enough. Songs live when kids sing them. Now every Sunday, twenty children come to the community hall and I teach them two songs. Last week, a nine-year-old taught her grandmother a song the grandmother had forgotten. The old lady cried. I cried too. That's why."

qa.q: How many songs has Nilesh recorded so far?
qa.a: Sixty songs.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when realising Dadi's songs weren't written down?
qa.a: Nilesh felt deeply saddened and shaken by the loss.

qa.q: What makes Nilesh's approach effective for preserving heritage?
qa.a: Recording elders and also teaching children weekly, so the songs are sung and passed on, not just stored.

qa.q: How might the grandmother have felt when her granddaughter taught her the forgotten song?
qa.a: She was moved to tears, likely feeling joy at recovering part of her past.

grounding: A young man describes recording elders' folk songs and teaching them to children to preserve cultural heritage.

passage: I'm Himani, and I teach at the same Pune school where Shreya, twenty-five, volunteers on Saturdays. This year I watched her run a project she called "Know Your City." She took Class 8 on walks to the old wada, the municipal office and a polling booth. She got a retired judge to explain how the constitution came to be, and asked the students to interview their grandparents about Partition and the old city. Then they made a small exhibition. On the last day, one shy boy stood up and said, "Now I want to vote when I turn eighteen." Shreya just nodded, but I saw her smile when she turned away. I don't know what she felt inside, but she stayed back cleaning up long after everyone left.

qa.q: What did Shreya call the project?
qa.a: "Know Your City."

qa.q: What might Shreya have felt when the shy boy spoke?
qa.a: She likely felt proud and moved, seeing the project reach a student.

qa.q: What made the project a good way to guide the next generation?
qa.a: It connected students to local heritage and institutions through visits, experts and interviews with grandparents.

qa.q: How does Himani see Shreya's work?
qa.a: Himani admires her quiet dedication, noticing her smile and how she stayed back to clean up.

grounding: A teacher observes a young volunteer teaching students about their city's heritage and civic institutions.

passage: I'm Raghav, Dhruv's neighbour in Dehradun. Dhruv's twenty-six. For the past year, I've seen him juggle everything. Every morning he helps his grandmother to the balcony, sets her tea and pills, and checks her blood pressure with the machine the doctor gave them. Then he goes to work, where he runs a solar project for mountain schools. On Sundays, three college juniors come to his flat, and he teaches them how to write project proposals. He also started a tree-planting group for our lane. I don't know how he doesn't collapse. Once I asked. He said, "Nani looked after me. The mountains looked after us. I'm just returning it." He laughed, but his eyes were tired.

passage: Hafsa Nani settled into her chair. "Imran, when I was twenty-five, about your age, I had more work than two hands could hold. My in-laws were old and sick; I looked after them both. I also ran the tailoring cooperative for our lane's women; twenty of them earned through it. And every monsoon, I got the children to plant neem saplings along the road. People said, 'Hafsa, you'll break.' Some days I nearly did. Then I learned to ask: I trained two younger women to run the co-op. I let my husband do the night shifts with his parents. I kept the trees for myself. Those neems are forty years old now." Imran looked out of the window at the huge trees. "Those?" "Those."

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, at twenty-five, she cared for in-laws, led a cooperative and planted trees by learning to share the load.
